metadata.scope: e_africa (all baronies across k_maghreb and k_tahert)

schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if not extracted from retrieved summary and flagged for manual check).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true if the barony title name is historically authentic for the 867 AD start date; false if anachronistic or unattested <= 867 (candidate for Step 2 resolution).
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person/dynasty/settler after 867 AD.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or other natural topographic feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with source language and English translation.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name STRICTLY ATTESTED <= 867 AD exists for the settlement (or its immediate predecessor site / base name without a post-867 modifier). Every exists=true entry carries first_mention_year <= 867.

b_tenerife.etymology_analysis: Derived from a Guanche (Berber-related) term, commonly interpreted as 'white mountain' (teni + ife) in reference to snow-capped Mount Teide; a 17th-century tradition also linked it to a legendary ruler Tinerfe.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Pliny the Elder recorded the island as Nivaria ('snowy', from Latin nix) in reference to Mount Teide; the indigenous Guanche name Achinech is only attested in post-1490s European chronicles.

b_grancanaria.first_mention_attestation: Le Canarien and 15th-century Castilian conquest chronicles (c. 1402–1483)

morphemes.translation: of dogs (from canis) or Canarii tribe

b_grancanaria.etymology_analysis: Compound of Spanish Gran ('great') and Latin Canaria, attested by Pliny the Elder (from canis, 'dog', or the North African Canarii people).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 AD, citing Juba II c. 40 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Pliny the Elder attested the island as Canaria; the Spanish qualifier 'Gran' was added in the 15th century. The indigenous name Tamaran is only recorded in post-conquest sources.

b_fuerteventura.first_mention_attestation: Angelino Dulcert's portolan chart (1339) as 'Forte Ventura'
b_fuerteventura.etymology_analysis: First recorded as Forte Ventura on the 1339 Dulcert chart, from Spanish fuerte ('strong') and ventura ('fortune', or associated with strong coastal winds / Fortunatae Insulae).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Pliny the Elder recorded the island as Planaria ('flat') and Capraria; indigenous Guanche names Erbania and Maxorata are attested only in 15th-century European chronicles.

b_lanzarote.first_mention_attestation: Angelino Dulcert's portolan chart (1339) as 'Insula de Lanzarotus Marocelus'
b_lanzarote.eponym_details: Named after the 14th-century Genoese navigator Lancelotto Malocello (fl. 1312–1339).
b_lanzarote.etymology_analysis: Derived from the given name of Genoese navigator Lancelotto Malocello, who landed on the island c. 1312 and appears on Dulcert's 1339 map.

older_name_by_867.notes: Known in antiquity only collectively with Fuerteventura as the Purpurariae (Purple Islands) in Pliny the Elder; the indigenous Guanche name Tyterogaka is attested only in the 15th-century chronicle Le Canarien.

b_madeira.first_mention_attestation: Portuguese royal charters and maps (1433) as 'Ilha da Madeira'
b_madeira.etymology_analysis: From Portuguese madeira ('wood, timber'), given by 15th-century Portuguese explorers for the island's dense primeval forests.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Madêre).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Pliny the Elder mentions the Purple Islands (Purpurariae), commonly identified with the Madeira archipelago.

b_fes.first_mention_attestation: Foundation of Madinat Fas by Idris I (789 AD)

morphemes.translation: pickaxe (Arabic fa's) or Berber afas ('ruins' / 'right bank')

b_fes.etymology_analysis: Traditionally linked to Arabic fa's ('pickaxe', from a legend of Idris I finding a gold pickaxe) or to Berber afas ('ruins' / 'right bank') or the nearby Fazaz region.

b_wargha.etymology_analysis: From the Berber hydronym Asif n Wergha (Arabic Wadi Wargha), the major northern tributary of the Sebou River.

b_warzigh.etymology_analysis: Obscure Moroccan toponym in the Fes region; no verified medieval attestation or etymology is documented.

b_al_aliya.first_mention_attestation: Foundation of al-Aliya by Idris II (809 AD) and Idrisid coinage
b_al_aliya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-'Aliya ('the High/Lofty'), founded by Idris II in 809 AD across the river from Madinat Fas and attested on Idrisid dirhams.

b_subu.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 AD) as 'Sububus'; Ptolemy as 'Subur'
b_subu.etymology_analysis: Ancient hydronym attested as Latin Sububus (Pliny) and Greek Subur (Ptolemy), preserved in Berber Asif n Sbu and Arabic Subu (Sebou).

b_sala.first_mention_attestation: Roman Sala Colonia (c. 40 AD) and Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150 AD) as 'Sala'
b_sala.etymology_analysis: Pre-Roman Punic/Berber settlement name Sala, Romanized as Sala Colonia (Chellah) and preserved in Arabic Sala (modern Salé).

b_al-basra.first_mention_attestation: Idrisid silver dirhams minted at al-Basra in 80 AH (796–797 AD)
b_al-basra.etymology_analysis: Founded by the Idrisids c. 796–800 AD and deliberately named after the port city of Basra in Iraq.

b_izerhan.first_mention_attestation: Mount Zerhoun attested in post-867 medieval Arabic geography; exact early date of 'Izerhan' unknown
b_izerhan.etymology_analysis: Berber form of Mount Zerhoun (Zarhun), the massif overlooking Volubilis where the town of Moulay Idriss Zerhoun developed.

b_watit.first_mention_attestation: Idrisid silver dirhams minted at Watit in 202 AH (818 AD) under Idris II
b_watit.etymology_analysis: Idrisid minting center attested on silver dirhams struck in 202 AH (818 AD) during the reign of Idris II.

b_walila.first_mention_attestation: Idris I's arrival at Walila (789 AD) and Idrisid dirhams minted at Walila (174 AH / 790–791 AD)
b_walila.etymology_analysis: Medieval Berber-Arabic name (Walila) for the ancient Mauretanian-Roman city of Volubilis.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 AD) and 1st-century Roman inscriptions
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman provincial capital of Mauretania Tingitana, continuously inhabited into the early Islamic period when it became known as Walila.

b_ribat_al-fath.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1150 AD by Almohad Caliph Abd al-Mu'min as Ribat al-Fath
b_ribat_al-fath.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ribat al-Fath ('Fortress of Victory'), founded in 1150 AD by the Almohads as a staging camp for campaigns in al-Andalus; shortened to Rabat.

b_meknes.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century settlement of Miknasat al-Zaytun by the Miknasa tribe
b_meknes.etymology_analysis: Named after the Zenata Berber tribe of the Miknasa (Imeknasen, from Berber root KNS 'to fight'), who settled the site in the 10th century.

b_baht.first_mention_attestation: River name Oued Beht/Baht attested in later medieval/modern geography; no pre-867 textual attestation
b_baht.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Oued Beht, a major tributary of the Sebou River rising in the Middle Atlas.

b_sefrou.first_mention_attestation: Idris II's residence at Sefrou (806–807 AD) and 9th-century Idrisid chronicles
b_sefrou.etymology_analysis: Named after the Berber Ahel Sefrou tribe or Amazigh Asfru ('solution/clearing'); already a notable town when Idris II stayed there in 806–807 AD.

b_tagragra.etymology_analysis: Amazigh toponym common in North Africa; unattested as a settlement in the Meknes region before 867 AD.

b_missour.first_mention_attestation: French military post established at Missour in July 1917
b_missour.etymology_analysis: Associated in local tradition with Arabic al-yusr ('prosperity, ease'); the modern town grew around a French post established in 1917.

b_tikoutamine.etymology_analysis: Berber village name in Boulemane Province (Middle Moulouya); unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD.

b_el_ksabi.etymology_analysis: Ksabi Moulouya, a rural settlement in Boulemane Province on the Moulouya River; unattested <= 867 AD.

b_taza.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Ribat Taza in the early 10th century (c. 920s) by Miknasa leader Musa ibn Abi'l-Afiya

morphemes.translation: from tizi ('mountain pass / hill between mountains')

b_taza.etymology_analysis: Derived from Amazigh tizi ('pass/col between mountains'); founded as a fortified ribat (Ribat Taza) in the early 10th century by the Miknasa.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Tâse — Historical Option A seat of c_taza

b_nador.first_mention_attestation: 19th-century foundation by local Berber tribes (Has Nador of Mazouza)
b_nador.etymology_analysis: Founded in the 19th century, named after the local Berber clan Has Nador (or Arabic al-nāẓūr, 'lookout').

older_name_by_867.notes: Nearby Melilla (ancient Rusadir) was attested in antiquity, but Nador itself was founded in the 19th century.

b_asfi.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Asfi (Europeanized as Safi), first attested in Islamic geographical sources by al-Bakri (11th century) and al-Idrisi (12th century).

b_aghuz.first_mention_attestation: al-Bakri (1068 AD) as 'Quz' (seaport of Aghmat); later Portuguese 'Aguz' (1506)

morphemes.translation: port / coastal settlement at the Tensift mouth

b_aghuz.etymology_analysis: Medieval coastal port at the mouth of the Tensift River (al-Bakri's Quz, later Aguz / Souira Guedima), attested from the 11th century.

b_igiradyatuf.etymology_analysis: Berber compound beginning with igir/ighir ('ridge, promontory'); unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD.

b_mrira.first_mention_attestation: Idrisid coin inscribed 'at Mrira, year 201 AH' (816–817 AD) found near Tighza/Mrirt
b_mrira.etymology_analysis: Medieval settlement (modern M'rirt) near the Tighza/Jbel Aouam mines, attested by a 201 AH (816–817 AD) coin reading 'at Mrira'.

b_el_borouj.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 attestation; modern center of the Beni Meskine tribe (arrived in Tamesna in the 14th century)
b_el_borouj.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-buruj ('the towers'), capital of the Beni Meskine tribe in Settat Province; unattested <= 867 AD.

b_tit-an-wagurramt.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym meaning 'spring of the saintly woman'; unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD.

b_marrakesh.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1070 AD by Almoravid leader Abu Bakr ibn Umar
b_marrakesh.etymology_analysis: Commonly derived from Amazigh Amur n Akush ('Land of God'); founded c. 1070 AD by the Almoravids as their imperial capital.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Achmât — Historical Option A seat of c_marrakesh

b_aitiyat.etymology_analysis: Berber tribal/clan name ('People of Iyat'); unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD.

b_aghmat.first_mention_attestation: al-Baladhuri (9th c., citing Musa ibn Nusayr's mosque c. 708) and Idris II's early 9th-century conquest
b_aghmat.etymology_analysis: Important early medieval Berber commercial town in the Haouz plain, attested in 9th-century Arabic historiography (al-Baladhuri) and Idrisid history.

b_ribat-shakir.first_mention_attestation: 12th-century Moroccan Sufi sources (where Abu Muhammad Salih studied under Abu Abdallah Mohammed Amghar)
b_ribat-shakir.etymology_analysis: Named after a Sufi ribat (modern Sidi Chiker); while later tradition links it to a 7th-century companion of Uqba ibn Nafi, contemporary historical attestation begins in the 12th century.

b_boulawan.first_mention_attestation: Kasbah Boulaouane commissioned c. 1710 AD by Sultan Moulay Ismail

morphemes.translation: place name on the Oum Er-Rbia

b_boulawan.etymology_analysis: Town and fortress overlooking the Oum Er-Rbia River, built around 1710 by Alaouite Sultan Moulay Ismail.

b_tadla.first_mention_attestation: Idrisid partition following the death of Idris II (828 AD), recorded by al-Bakri (1068 AD)
b_tadla.etymology_analysis: From Amazigh tadla ('sheaf of wheat'), referring to the fertile cereal-producing plain; attested as an Idrisid province in the early 9th century.

b_dai.first_mention_attestation: Idrisid partition of 828 AD (assigned to Idris II's son Yahya), recorded by al-Bakri (1068 AD)
b_dai.etymology_analysis: Medieval mining and urban center in Tadla (near modern Beni Mellal), recorded by al-Bakri as an Idrisid principality from 828 AD.

b_wazeqqur.etymology_analysis: Obscure Berber toponym in the Tadla region; unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD.

b_wawmana.etymology_analysis: Modern rural commune (Ouaoumana) in Khénifra Province; unattested in historical sources <= 867 AD.

b_afza.etymology_analysis: Medieval Tadla settlement mentioned by al-Idrisi (12th century) near Bzou/Dai; Berber afza refers to limestone rock.

b_aititab.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 or medieval Arabic geographical sources; modern valley and Berber tribal confederation in Azilal Province.
b_aititab.etymology_analysis: Berber tribal ethnonym meaning 'descendants/clan of Attab', applied to an agricultural valley in the Central High Atlas.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ait i Tab (constituent holding of Tadle)

b_anfa.first_mention_attestation: Roman commercial port of Anfus/Anfa established under Augustus c. 15 BCE on an earlier Berber settlement.
b_anfa.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym meaning 'hill' (Latinized as Anfus in Roman times), referring to the coastal elevation of old Casablanca; later replaced by Casablanca / ad-Dar al-Bayda after the 1755 earthquake.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_fadala.first_mention_attestation: First attested by al-Idrisi in Nuzhat al-mushtaq (1154 AD) as an Atlantic anchorage.
b_fadala.etymology_analysis: Arabic toponym Fadala (from Fadl Allah 'favor of God' or Fayd Allah 'bounty of God'), renamed Mohammedia in 1959-1960 after King Mohammed V.

older_name_by_867.notes: No classical or pre-867 settlement name is attested at the site.

b_azzamur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Azammur in medieval Arabic geography (al-Idrisi, 1154 AD).
b_azzamur.etymology_analysis: From Berber azemmur ('wild olive tree'), adopted into Arabic as Azammur.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Punic/Roman coastal toponym Azama / Asama
older_name_by_867.notes: Azemmour is generally identified with the ancient Punic trading post of Azama (Latinized as Asama).

b_mazaghan.first_mention_attestation: First documented as Mazighan by al-Bakri in Kitab al-Masalik wa-l-Mamalik (1068 AD).
b_mazaghan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Berber-Arabic coastal name Mazighan (Portuguese Mazagao, later renamed El Jadida in 1820).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy, Geography (2nd century AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Identified with the classical anchorage of Rusibis (later also called Portus Rutilis).

b_tinmallal.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a ribat in 1124 AD by Ibn Tumart, founder of the Almohad movement.
b_tinmallal.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Tinmal / Tinmallal meaning 'the white one', founded by Ibn Tumart in the High Atlas in 1124.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Tinmel founded 1124. Pre-867 Berber valley of the Oued N'fis.

older_name_by_867.notes: Situated in the Oued N'fis valley, but Tinmel itself was established in 1124.

b_tasgimut.first_mention_attestation: Fortress constructed under Almoravid emir Ali ibn Yusuf by 1125 AD to defend Aghmat.
b_tasgimut.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym for the rocky plateau fortress near Aghmat built by the Almoravids in the 1120s and taken by the Almohads in 1132.

b_naffis.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by Idris II (r. 803-828 AD) alongside Aghmat c. 814-825 AD; later described by al-Bakri (1068).
b_naffis.etymology_analysis: Berber hydronym and settlement name for the Oued N'fis valley and town in the High Atlas foothills south of Marrakesh.

b_sabta.first_mention_attestation: Arabic form Sabta adopted during the Umayyad conquest of the Maghreb (c. 709-711 AD) from Latin Septem.
b_sabta.etymology_analysis: Arabic adaptation of Latin Septem (short for Septem Fratres, 'Seven Brothers', referring to the seven hills of Ceuta).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek/Punic Abyla (5th c. BCE) and Roman Septem Fratres (1st c. CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Phoenician/Punic Abyla preceded Roman Septem (Septem Fratres), which became Arabic Sabta.

b_tittawan.first_mention_attestation: First explicitly attested in extant writing by al-Bakri (1068 AD), though inhabited under the Idrisids in the 9th century.
b_tittawan.etymology_analysis: Berber plural noun tittawin meaning 'eyes' or 'water springs', Arabized as Titwan / Tetouan.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ancient Mauretanian and Roman town of Tamuda (3rd century BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Tamuda stood a few kilometers outside modern Tetouan.

b_ghumira.first_mention_attestation: Ghomara (Ghumara) confederation attested in the Berber Revolt of 739-740 AD and the 828 Idrisid partition.
b_ghumira.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and regional choronym of the Ghomara (Berber Ighmaren), a Masmuda Berber confederation inhabiting the western Rif.

b_melilla.first_mention_attestation: Repopulated by Berbers c. 890 AD under the name Malilya / Melilla before Umayyad seizure in 926-927.
b_melilla.etymology_analysis: Arabic Malilya (Spanish Melilla), likely derived from the Berber root M-L-L ('white').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Phoenician/Punic Rusaddir and Roman Rusadir (Pliny the Elder)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Phoenician colony Rusaddir ('mighty cape'), later Roman colony Rusadir.

b_nakur.first_mention_attestation: Madinat al-Nakur founded between 749 and 761 AD by Idris ibn Salih as capital of the Emirate of Nekor.
b_nakur.etymology_analysis: Named after the Nekor River in the Rif; capital of the Salihid Emirate of Nekor (raided by Vikings in 859 AD).

b_tangiers.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Punic, Greek, and Roman sources as Tingis/Tinga from at least the 5th century BCE (settled earlier by Phoenicians).
b_tangiers.etymology_analysis: From ancient Berber/Punic Tingi (Latin Tingis, Arabic Tanja, English Tangier/Tangiers).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Classical Greek, Punic, and Roman sources (Tingis / Tingi)
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical form Tingis/Tingi is the direct ancestor of Arabic Tanja and English Tangiers.

b_asila.first_mention_attestation: Raided by Vikings (al-Majus) in 844 AD under the Idrisid dynasty, as recorded in Arabic chronicles.
b_asila.etymology_analysis: Idrisid-era coastal town whose name Asila (and Spanish/Portuguese Arzila) derives from the nearby ancient Phoenician-Roman settlement of Zilis/Zilil.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Phoenician-Roman site at Dchar Jdid (Zilis / Zilil)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Zilis/Zilil lies 12 km northeast of modern Asilah.

b_kasr_al-kabir.first_mention_attestation: Fortified and renamed al-Qasr al-Kabir ('the Great Castle') under Almohad caliph Yaqub al-Mansur in the late 12th century.
b_kasr_al-kabir.etymology_analysis: Arabic descriptive name 'the Great Castle' (Spanish Alcazarquivir), succeeding earlier medieval names Suq Kutama and Qasr Abd al-Karim.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Ksar el-Kebir / Qasr al-Kabir (Arabic 'The Great Castle / Citadel') (in-game: Grôzcastel)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive Arabic fortress toponym calqued to Tarraconian Grôzcastel.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Mauretania Tingitana settlement Oppidum Novum
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Oppidum Novum occupied the strategic crossing on the Loukkos River.

b_tahlit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 or medieval historical sources; minor modern locality in northern Morocco.
b_tahlit.etymology_analysis: Local Moroccan toponym with no documented pre-modern attestation.

b_agadir.first_mention_attestation: Urban settlement founded in 1505 AD by the Portuguese as Santa Cruz do Cabo de Gue; local Berber name Agadir attested in the 16th century.
b_agadir.etymology_analysis: From Tashelhit Berber agadir ('wall' or 'fortified collective granary'); full name Agadir Ighir.

current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Anachronistic foundation evaluated in 1059 Imperial Chancellery audit.

b_massa.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned by Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, c. 77 AD) as the river Masatat and people Masates; medieval port and ribat of Massa described by al-Ya'qubi (891 AD).
b_massa.etymology_analysis: Pre-Islamic Berber hydronym and tribal name (Pliny's Masatat / Masates), preserved in the Oued Massa and the medieval ribat/port of Massa.

b_tazagourt.first_mention_attestation: Almoravid fortress constructed on Mount Zagora (Tazagourt) in the late 11th century.
b_tazagourt.etymology_analysis: Berber oronym Tazagurt ('twin peaks') naming the double-peaked Mount Zagora, later Arabized as Zagora.

b_al-talha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 or medieval Arabic geographical sources; minor oasis settlement in Draa-Tafilalet.
b_al-talha.etymology_analysis: Arabic descriptive botanical toponym meaning 'the acacia tree'.

b_aqqa.first_mention_attestation: Emerges in historical records in the 16th century under the Saadian dynasty, replacing the nearby medieval town of Tamdult.
b_aqqa.etymology_analysis: From Tamazight aqqa meaning 'dates' or 'date kernel', reflecting the oasis's palm groves.

older_name_by_867.notes: Nearby medieval Tamdult (13 km SW) dates to the 9th-11th centuries but is a distinct site.

b_tagmadart.first_mention_attestation: Town of Tagmadert founded in 1550 AD by Saadian sultan Mohammed ash-Sheikh.

morphemes.translation: Berber oasis/district name in the Draa

b_tagmadart.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym in the Draa Valley (also Tagumadert), associated with the origins of the Saadian dynasty.

b_tidri.first_mention_attestation: Medieval hilltop settlement site in the Middle Draa Valley; the name Tidri is unattested in pre-867 written sources.
b_tidri.etymology_analysis: Berber settlement name in the Middle Draa oasis zone (Foum Tidri).

b_ifni.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1860 Treaty of Tangiers (later Sidi Ifni); unattested in pre-867 or medieval sources.
b_ifni.etymology_analysis: From Tashelhit Berber ifni ('basin' or 'lagoon/plain'), later prefixed with Sidi ('saint/lord').

b_nul_lamta.first_mention_attestation: Founded around the 8th century as a trans-Saharan caravan city in the Asrir/Tighmert oasis; described by al-Bakri (11th c.).
b_nul_lamta.etymology_analysis: Named after the oasis/wadi of Nul (Noun) and the Lamta Berber tribe, famous in medieval trade for Lamta shields.

b_taghmut.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 or medieval written sources; modern oasis village in the Anti-Atlas.
b_taghmut.etymology_analysis: Local Tashelhit Berber toponym in the Anti-Atlas mountains.

b_assa.first_mention_attestation: Zaouia of Assa founded in the 13th century (c. 1250 AD) by Sheikh Izza Wahidi.
b_assa.etymology_analysis: Berber oasis toponym in southern Morocco, known historically for its 13th-century religious zawiya and ksar.

b_tagawst.first_mention_attestation: Emerged as a major trans-Saharan caravan town in the 13th century (succeeding Nul Lamta) and described by Leo Africanus (16th c.).
b_tagawst.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym in the Oued Noun / Guelmim plain (also spelled Tagaost or Taghaost) that served as a major caravan terminus from the 13th to 17th centuries.

b_iligh.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the capital of the Emirate/Kingdom of Tazeroualt in 1626 AD by Ali Abu Hassun al-Simlali.
b_iligh.etymology_analysis: Tashelhit Berber toponym for the 17th-century maraboutic capital of Tazerwalt in the Anti-Atlas.

b_tarudant.first_mention_attestation: Conquered by the Almoravids in 1056 AD; earliest securely dated historical attestation of Taroudant.
b_tarudant.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (Arabic Tarudant) for the chief town of the Sous valley from the 11th century onward.

older_name_by_867.notes: Speculatively linked to ancient Vala/Uala, but unconfirmed.

b_igilliz.first_mention_attestation: Birthplace of Almohad founder Ibn Tumart (c. 1080 AD) and fortified ribat from 1121 AD.
b_igilliz.etymology_analysis: From Tashelhit Berber igiliz ('mountain spur' or 'summit'), describing the fortified rocky outcrop in the Anti-Atlas.

b_sirwan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Moroccan sources by the 13th century (Jbel Siroua / Sirwan).
b_sirwan.etymology_analysis: Berber oronym (Jbel Siroua / Sirwan) for the volcanic massif linking the High Atlas and Anti-Atlas.

b_sijilmasa.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 757 AD by Sufrite Kharijites / Banu Midrar on the Ziz River.
b_sijilmasa.etymology_analysis: Medieval Islamic city name (Arabic Sijilmasa), founded in 757 AD as the premier northern entrepot of the western trans-Saharan trade.

b_tafilalt.first_mention_attestation: Appears as the regional oasis name Tafilalt in the 14th century, gradually replacing Sijilmasa.
b_tafilalt.etymology_analysis: Berber word tafilalt meaning 'earthenware jug' used to store water, applied to the oasis region from the late Middle Ages.

b_taouz.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 or medieval written sources; desert village on the Oued Ziz near prehistoric rock art sites.
b_taouz.etymology_analysis: Berber oasis toponym on the lower Oued Ziz with no pre-modern documentary attestation.

b_tudgha.first_mention_attestation: Abbasid silver dirhams minted at Tudgha under Yazid ibn Hatim, governor of Ifriqiya (771-787 AD).
b_tudgha.etymology_analysis: Berber hydronym and oasis name (Arabic Tudgha) in southeastern Morocco, active as an early Islamic silver-mining and minting center in the 8th century.

b_tasagdah.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Tasagdalt, a stone fortress near Sijilmasa to which Midrarid emir Muhammad ibn al-Fath fled c. 909-913 AD.

morphemes.translation: stone fortress / plateau (identified with Gara Medouar)

b_tasagdah.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (Tasagdalt) recorded in early 10th-century Midrarid history, identified by archaeologists with the fortified massif of Gara Medouar.

b_warzazat.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned by al-Bakri in Kitab al-Masalik wa-l-Mamalik (1068 AD) as a territory of the Haskoura tribe.
b_warzazat.etymology_analysis: Tashelhit Berber compound War-zazat ('without noise'), originally naming a quiet widening of the Oued Ouarzazate riverbed before becoming a town name.

b_ziz.first_mention_attestation: River Ziz (Wadi Ziz) attested in medieval Arabic geographical works beginning with al-Bakri (1068 AD) and al-Idrisi (1154 AD).
b_ziz.etymology_analysis: Berber hydronym (Asif n Ziz, Arabic Wadi Ziz) for the major river feeding the Tafilalt oasis.

b_ghazwan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement in the Ziz/Tafilalt region.
b_ghazwan.etymology_analysis: Arabic personal/tribal name used as a barony title without documented pre-867 or medieval attestation in the Ziz valley.

b_algiers.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 944–972 AD by Zirid ruler Buluggin ibn Ziri as al-Jaza'ir Bani Mazghanna; attested by Ibn Hawqal (c. 977) and al-Bakri (1068).
b_algiers.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Jaza'ir ('the islands'), referring to the four offshore islets in the Bay of Algiers (full medieval name al-Jaza'ir Bani Mazghanna), via Catalan Alguer and French Alger.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Historic Zirid island fortress al-Jazā'ir (Algiers) (in-game: Alschîr)

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Punic coins (Ikosim, 2nd–1st century BCE) and Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia V.20 (77 AD, as Icosium).
older_name_by_867.notes: Phoenician-Punic trading post and later Roman colony on the exact site of modern Algiers.

b_medea.first_mention_attestation: Refounded in the mid-10th century (c. 944–960 AD) by Zirid prince Buluggin ibn Ziri as al-Madiya.

morphemes.translation: Medea (adaptation of Roman ad Medias / Lamdia)

b_medea.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Madiya (French Medea), adapted from the Roman way-station ad Medias ('halfway' between Tirinadi and Sufnsar) or the ancient settlement/tribe name Lamdia/Lambdia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Conference of Carthage (411 AD, Donatist bishop Felix of Lamdia) and Roman itineraries (ad Medias).
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman military post and Christian bishopric in Mauretania Caesariensis on the site later refounded by Buluggin ibn Ziri.

b_tadallis.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tedles / Tadallis by al-Idrisi in Nuzhat al-Mushtaq (1154 AD).
b_tadallis.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Tadallis / Tedelles (modern Dellys), likely formed with feminine prefix ta- and adles (a riverside reed/grass, Ampelodesmos mauritanicus).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia V.20 (77 AD), and Christian bishopric lists (411, 484 AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Phoenician colony and Roman municipium in Mauretania Caesariensis at the site of modern Dellys.

b_mattija.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Arabic historiography and geography (al-Bakri, 11th century; later Ibn Khaldun) as the Mitidja plain.
b_mattija.etymology_analysis: From Berber Mettijet / Mattija, traditionally derived from Berber itij ('sun, shining'), meaning 'the sunny (plain)'.

b_tanas.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Tanas (Tenes) founded in 875–876 AD (262 AH) by Andalusian mariners according to al-Bakri.
b_tanas.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tanas (French Tenes), from Berber root TNS meaning 'to camp' or 'encampment', applied to the 9th-century Andalusian foundation.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia V.20 (77 AD) and Ptolemy, Geography IV.2 (2nd century AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Phoenician port and Roman colony (Cartennae) located 3.2 km from the medieval 875 AD foundation of Tanas.

b_sharshal.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Sharshal in 10th–11th century Arabic geography (Ibn Hawqal, 977 AD; al-Bakri, 1068 AD).
b_sharshal.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sharshal (French Cherchell), either a phonological evolution of Latin Caesarea or derived from Berber achercher/shersher ('waterfall').

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax (4th century BCE, as Iol) and Juba II / Pliny Naturalis Historia V.20 (renamed Caesarea in 25 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Punic trading port Iol, later capital of Mauretania under Juba II as Caesarea.

b_miliyana.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 10th century (c. 970s AD) by Zirid prince Buluggin ibn Ziri as Miliyana.
b_miliyana.etymology_analysis: Arabic Miliyana (French Miliana), founded by Buluggin ibn Ziri in the 10th century on the ruins of Roman Zucchabar; name possibly connected to a Latin gentilicium Malliana.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia V.21 (77 AD) and Ptolemy, Geography IV.2.
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta Zucchabar) in Mauretania Caesariensis on the exact site of modern Miliana.

b_bejaia.first_mention_attestation: Refounded/expanded in 1067 AD by Hammadid ruler al-Nasir ibn Alennas as al-Nasiriya, soon known as Bijaya (Bejaia) after the local Bajaya Berber tribe.
b_bejaia.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Bijaya / Kabyle Bgayet, named after the Bajaya Berber tribe (who inhabited the region prior to the Hammadid expansion in 1067).

current_repo_state.b_origin: Sâlde — Historical Option A seat of c_bejaia

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica XVII (c. 20 AD) and Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia V.20 (77 AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Carthaginian port and Roman veteran colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta Saldae) on the site of Bejaia.

b_jijel.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Arabic geography as Jijil / Jijel (al-Bakri, 1068 AD; al-Idrisi, 1154 AD).
b_jijel.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jijil / Kabyle Jijel, a medieval phonological contraction of the Punic-Roman toponym Igilgili.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia V.20 (77 AD) and Antonine Itinerary (3rd century AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Phoenician trading post and Roman colony in Mauretania Sitifensis.

b_satif.first_mention_attestation: Arabic form Satif attested in early Islamic geographers (al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan, 891 AD; later al-Bakri, 1068 AD).

morphemes.translation: black land (from Berber zdif / Latin Sitifis)

b_satif.etymology_analysis: Arabic Satif (French Setif), adapted from Latin Sitifis, which itself derives from a Numidian-Berber root zdif meaning 'black (fertile) lands'.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman foundation inscriptions of Colonia Nerviana Augusta Martialis Veteranorum Sitifensium (96–98 AD).
older_name_by_867.notes: Numidian settlement and Roman capital of Mauretania Sitifensis.

b_mila_satif.first_mention_attestation: Compound title 'Mila Satif' is a modern/cartographic disambiguation combining historic Mila with Satif; not attested as a single title <= 867 AD.
b_mila_satif.etymology_analysis: Combines Mila (from ancient Milevum, fortified by Justinian in the 6th century and conquered by Umayyads c. 675 AD) with Satif as a regional qualifier.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy, Geography IV.3.7 (2nd century AD, as Mileum) and Umayyad conquest accounts (c. 675–682 AD, as Mila).
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Numidian and Roman city of Milevum (Arabized as Mila), without the modern 'Satif' disambiguator.

b_ikjan.first_mention_attestation: First attested as the Kutama Berber stronghold and Fatimid dar al-hijra of Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i in 902–909 AD (Qadi al-Nu'man, Iftitah al-Da'wa, 957 AD).
b_ikjan.etymology_analysis: Berber (Kutama) toponym Ikjan (Ikedjane), a fortified mountain settlement near Beni Aziz that served as the first Fatimid base in 902–909 AD.

b_qalaa_bhammad.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1007–1008 AD (398 AH) by Hammad ibn Buluggin as Qal'at Bani Hammad.
b_qalaa_bhammad.eponym_details: Named after Hammad ibn Buluggin (d. 1028 AD), founder of the Hammadid dynasty.
b_qalaa_bhammad.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qal'at Bani Hammad ('Citadel of the Sons of Hammad'), the fortified palatine capital built by Hammad ibn Buluggin in 1007–1008 AD.

b_arigh.first_mention_attestation: Oued Righ / Arigh oasis region attested in medieval Arabic sources from the 12th–13th centuries (e.g., Yaqut al-Hamawi, Ibn Khaldun).
b_arigh.etymology_analysis: From Berber Arigh / Wadi Righ, named after the Zenata Berber tribe of the Righa (fraction of the Maghraoua), or per Yaqut al-Hamawi a Berber word for a salt marsh (sabkha).

b_ajlu.first_mention_attestation: Minor oasis/settlement in the Oued Righ region; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 AD.
b_ajlu.etymology_analysis: Local Saharan oasis toponym in the Oued Righ basin with no documented pre-867 attestation.

b_tuggurt.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ibn Khaldun (late 14th century) and as capital of the Sultanate of Touggourt founded in 1414 AD.
b_tuggurt.etymology_analysis: From Berber Tugurt (Tifinagh: ⵜⵓⴳⵓⵔⵜ), meaning 'the gate' or 'the gateway', referring to its strategic position at the entrance of the Oued Righ oasis chain.

b_ghardaia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the mid-11th century (c. 1048–1053 AD) by Ibadi Mozabite Berbers in the M'zab valley.

morphemes.translation: castle / fortified hilltop (or cave of Daia)

b_ghardaia.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ghardaia, from Tumzabt Berber Tagherdayt, linked either to Berber tagherda ('castle/fortress') or popular tradition 'cave (ghar) of Daia'.

b_al-qulaya.first_mention_attestation: Ksar of El Goléa (al-Qulay'a, now El Menia) built in the 10th century AD by Zenata Berbers.
b_al-qulaya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qulay'a (French El Goléa), diminutive of qal'a ('fortress'), meaning 'the little fortress', referring to the 10th-century Zenata hilltop ksar.

b_tedmait.first_mention_attestation: Tademait plateau in the central Algerian Sahara; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 AD.

morphemes.translation: palm of the hand / dwarf palm

b_tedmait.etymology_analysis: Berber Tadmayt / Tademait, meaning 'palm (of the hand)' or 'dwarf palm', applied to the hyper-arid Saharan plateau south of El Menia.

b_al-aghwat.first_mention_attestation: Traces its history to at least the 11th century AD; mentioned by Ibn Khaldun (14th century) in connection with the Zenata Banu Laghwat.

morphemes.translation: the gardens (Arabic pl. of ghouta) or saw-toothed mountain / Laghouat tribe (Berber)

b_al-aghwat.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Aghwat (French Laghouat), interpreted either as Arabic plural of ghouta ('oasis gardens') or as an Arabization of Berber Leghwat / agwath (Zenata tribe or serrated mountains).

b_tilghemt.first_mention_attestation: Saharan locality/depression south of Laghouat (near Hassi R'Mel); unattested in historical sources on or before 867 AD.
b_tilghemt.etymology_analysis: From Berber tilghemt ('she-camel', feminine of alghom), a Saharan toponym in Laghouat Province with no pre-867 attestation.

b_wargla.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century Arabic and Ibadi sources (e.g., Ibn Hawqal, 977 AD) as Warjlan / Wargla, flourishing after 909 AD when Ibadi refugees from Tahert settled there.
b_wargla.etymology_analysis: From Berber Wargren / Warjlan (Arabic Warqalah, French Ouargla), named after the Zenata Banu Wargla tribe or meaning 'he who is barricaded'.

b_taghyart.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Ibadi biographical collections (al-Wisiyani's Siyar, 12th century); unattested on or before 867 AD.
b_taghyart.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Taghyart associated with medieval Ibadi communities of the Sahara/Nafusa; not attested prior to 867 AD.

b_sadrata.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 909 AD by Ibadi refugees fleeing the Fatimid conquest of Tahert, taking its name from the Sedrata Berber tribe.
b_sadrata.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sedrata (Isedraten), a Zenata Berber tribe around Ouargla that sheltered Rustamid Ibadi refugees after 909 AD.

b_karima.first_mention_attestation: Garat Krima / Krima locality near Ouargla; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 AD.
b_karima.etymology_analysis: Modern/local Saharan toponym (Garat Krima) south of Ouargla with no documented attestation <= 867 AD.

b_ashir_yashir.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 935–936 AD by Ziri ibn Manad as the first Zirid capital (citadel of Yashir at Achir).

morphemes.translation: original Zirid citadel site at Achir

b_ashir_yashir.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Achir/Ashir (Acir), paired with Yashir, the original 935–936 AD palatial citadel built by Ziri ibn Manad in the Titteri Mountains.

b_bousaada.first_mention_attestation: Oasis town (ksar) established in the late medieval / early modern period (traditionally 15th–16th century).
b_bousaada.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Bu Sa'ada ('place of happiness'), an oasis caravan town on the northern edge of the Sahara.

b_ashir_banya.first_mention_attestation: Palatial citadel of Banya (Benia / Buniya) at Achir, founded in 974–978 AD by Buluggin ibn Ziri next to his father's foundation.
b_ashir_banya.etymology_analysis: Combines the Zirid capital name Ashir with Banya (Arabic buniya, 'structure/edifice'), the second palatial complex founded by Buluggin ibn Ziri in 974–978 AD.

b_sersou.first_mention_attestation: High plateau in western Algeria (near Tiaret); documented in 19th-century colonial records and unattested on or before 867 AD.
b_sersou.etymology_analysis: From Zenati Berber sers ('descend') + demonstrative suffix -u, meaning 'descending land' or 'plateau'.

b_figuig.first_mention_attestation: Oasis of Figuig attested in medieval Arabic and Maghrebi sources (12th–14th centuries, e.g., Ibn Khaldun); unattested on or before 867 AD.

morphemes.translation: mountain pass (or Zenati Berber oasis toponym)

b_figuig.etymology_analysis: From Zenati Berber Ifiyyey / Figig (Arabic Figuig), variously linked to a Berber toponym or Arabic fajj ('mountain pass').

b_ainsefra.first_mention_attestation: Ksar of Ain Sefra founded around 1586 AD by the descendants of Mohamed Benchaib (Bou Dekhil); modern town established as a French garrison in 1881–1882.
b_ainsefra.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Ayn al-Safra ('yellow spring'), referring to the desert spring at the oasis.

b_mecheria.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1881 AD as a French fortified military post and railway station on the Oran–Bechar line.
b_mecheria.etymology_analysis: From an Arabic term meaning 'place of dryness' or 'arid land', describing the semi-arid High Plateaus steppe where the 1881 post was built.

b_tahart.first_mention_attestation: Founded as the Rustamid capital in 761 AD by Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam (with earlier 7th-century Arab-era references to Tahart following Roman/Byzantine Tingartia).
b_tahart.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Tahert/Tihert (modern Tiaret), traditionally glossed as 'lioness' or 'station', adopted by the Rustamid imamate in 761 AD near the Roman-Byzantine site of Tingartia.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman and Byzantine provincial records of Mauretania Caesariensis
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman station and fort Tingartia occupied the citadel site of Old Tahert (Tiaret), while Rustamid New Tahert (Tagdemt) lay 10 km west.

b_al_ubbad.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1198 AD as the village of al-'Ubbad near Tlemcen where the Sufi master Abu Madyan (Sidi Boumediene) was buried.
b_al_ubbad.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-'Ubbad ('the worshippers/devotees'), a historic village on the outskirts of Tlemcen that grew into a major Sufi pilgrimage center around the tomb of Abu Madyan (d. 1198).

b_qalaa_bsalama.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Ibn Khaldun's autobiography and Kitab al-'Ibar (1375-1379 AD), where he composed the Muqaddimah at Qal'at ibn Salama / Qal'at Bani Salama.
b_qalaa_bsalama.eponym_details: Named after Ibn Salama / Banu Salama, the medieval Arab-Berber clan or founder associated with the mountain fortress near Taoughzout (Frenda), attested in 1375 AD.
b_qalaa_bsalama.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound Qal'at Bani Salama ('Fortress of the Banu Salama'), a hilltop stronghold near Taoughzout south of Frenda in Tiaret Province.

b_askedal.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 12th-century Maghrebi geographical sources (such as Kitab al-Istibsar / al-Idrisi) as Tasqadalt / Askedal, a fortified mountain settlement in western Algeria.
b_askedal.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Askedal (Tasqadalt), recorded in medieval Arabic geographical works alongside Madinat al-Jabal and Qal'at Hawwara in the Tell Atlas of western Algeria.

b_hisn_lawata.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 281 AH / 894 AD in Rustamid chronicles (al-Shammakhi, Ibn Khaldun), when Imam Abu Hatim Yusuf fled Tahert to Hisn Lawata.
b_hisn_lawata.etymology_analysis: Arabic-Berber compound Hisn Lawata ('Fortress of the Lawata'), referring to a stronghold of the Lawata Berber confederation in the Tahert region.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Hisn Lawata (Berber Lawata tribal fortress) (in-game: Lawâtaburch)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Descriptive Berber fortress toponym calqued to Tarraconian Lawâtaburch.

b_yalala.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Arabic geographical sources (al-Bakri, 1068 AD) as Madinat Yellel / Yalala in western Algeria.
b_yalala.etymology_analysis: From Berber ilel ('sea, lake'), designating the medieval town of Yellel in Relizane Province, built on the Roman site of Ballene Praesidium.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman provincial itinerary of Mauretania Caesariensis
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman military station Ballene Praesidium occupied the site of modern Yellel.

b_qalaa_bhuwara.first_mention_attestation: Established by the Hawwara Berbers in the Mina valley during the late 8th to early 9th century (reign of Rustamid Imam Abd al-Wahhab, 784-824 AD) as Qal'at Hawwara.
b_qalaa_bhuwara.etymology_analysis: Arabic-Berber Qal'at Hawwara ('Fortress of the Hawwara'), later renamed Kalaa des Beni Rached; founded by the Hawwara tribe in the Mina valley under Rustamid suzerainty.

b_al_gabal.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Arabic geographical sources (e.g., al-Bakri, 1068 AD) as Madinat al-Jabal ('City of the Mountain'), an alternate name for Qal'at Hawwara.
b_al_gabal.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Jabal ('the Mountain'), a descriptive oronymic designation applied in medieval sources to the mountain stronghold near Relizane.

b_hunyan.first_mention_attestation: Fortified and attested in the 12th century AD under the Almohad Caliph Abd al-Mu'min as the port of Honaine (Hunayn).
b_hunyan.etymology_analysis: Medieval Maghrebi port name Hunayn (Honaine), developed as Tlemcen's maritime outlet under the Almohads on the site of Roman Gypsaria.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Conference of Carthage (411 AD) and Roman itineraries of Mauretania Caesariensis
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman coastal town and bishopric Gypsaria (Gissaria) / Artisiga preceded medieval Honaine.

b_arsgul.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 10th century AD under the Sulaymanid dynasty (Idris ibn Ibrahim, chief of Arshgul) and described by al-Bakri in 1068 AD.

morphemes.translation: hill or garden (or adaptation of Siga)

b_arsgul.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabized form Arshgul (modern Rachgoun), derived from Punic-Berber Rus-gun / Rus-Siga, occupying the site of ancient Siga at the mouth of the Tafna.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Numidian coinage (Shigan) and classical accounts of King Syphax (206 BC)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Masaesyli capital Siga and Roman port Portus Sigensis occupied the exact site of medieval Arshgul.

b_nadruma.first_mention_attestation: First explicitly mentioned in 1068 AD by the Andalusi geographer al-Bakri in Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik.

morphemes.translation: Berber toponym of the Trara region

b_nadruma.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Nadruma (Nedroma), capital of the Trara mountains, first attested in 1068 AD and fortified under the Almoravids and Almohads.

older_name_by_867.notes: Built on the ruins of an earlier unnamed Berber settlement.

b_oran.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 903 AD by Andalusi sailors alongside the Azdadja and Ajissa Berbers of the Maghrawa confederation.
b_oran.etymology_analysis: From Berber Wahran ('two lions', plural of wahra), Arabized as Wahran and Frenchified as Oran, founded in 903 AD near the vanished Roman settlement of Unica Colonia.

current_repo_state.b_origin: Wahrân — Historical Option A seat of c_orania

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman provincial records of Mauretania Caesariensis
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman settlement Unica Colonia existed in the area of modern Oran prior to its abandonment in Late Antiquity.

b_marsafarukh.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century Arabic geographical accounts (Ibn Hawqal, c. 988 AD) as Marsa Farrukh, the Mediterranean port serving Tahert.
b_marsafarukh.etymology_analysis: Arabic Marsa Farrukh ('Port of Farrukh'), a coastal anchorage on the western Algerian littoral that served as a maritime outlet for Rustamid Tahert.

b_arzew.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned c. 1068 AD by al-Bakri as Arzao, referring to the abandoned Roman ruins of Portus Magnus.
b_arzew.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Arzao (modern Arzew), first recorded in 1068 AD by al-Bakri at the site of the ruined Roman port of Portus Magnus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Empire (Mauretania Caesariensis); destroyed by Vandals in 429-430 AD
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman colony Portus Magnus ('Great Port') at nearby Bethioua preceded medieval Arzao (Arzew).

b_tlemcen.first_mention_attestation: Attested on Rustamid silver fulus coins struck at Tilimsan under Abd al-Wahhab (784-824 AD) and in al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (891 AD).
b_tlemcen.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Tilimsan ('springs'), emerging in the 8th-9th centuries alongside Agadir (790 AD) on the ruins of Roman Pomaria, later merged with Almoravid Tagrart (1082 AD).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman military outpost Pomaria (2nd century AD; Council of Carthage 411 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Pomaria ('Orchards') was renamed Agadir in Berber (refounded by Idris I in 790 AD) before merging with Tagrart as Tlemcen.

b_muaskar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 10th century AD by the Banu Ifran Berbers as Mu'askar (modern Mascara).

morphemes.translation: military camp / place where soldiers gather

b_muaskar.etymology_analysis: Arabic Mu'askar ('encampment / garrison', later Frenchified as Mascara), founded in the 10th century by the Banu Ifran.

b_qasr-ibn-sinan.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1068 AD by al-Bakri as Qasr Ibn Sinan ('Castle of Ibn Sinan'), a fortified settlement of the Azdadja Berbers between Oran and Tlemcen.
b_qasr-ibn-sinan.eponym_details: Named after Ibn Sinan of the Azdadja Berber tribe, founder/lord of the castle recorded by al-Bakri (1068 AD).
b_qasr-ibn-sinan.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound Qasr Ibn Sinan ('Castle of Ibn Sinan'), located near Aïn Témouchent and attested by al-Bakri in 1068 AD.

b_aintekbalet.first_mention_attestation: Modern village name in Tlemcen Province; Roman-era travertine quarries existed nearby from the 2nd century AD without attestation of the name Aïn Tekbalet.
b_aintekbalet.etymology_analysis: Arabic-Berber compound 'Ayn Tekbalet ('Spring of Tekbalet'), a modern locality in northwestern Algeria known for its ancient alabaster/travertine quarries.

b_tafraoua-sebdou.first_mention_attestation: Known as Tafraoua prior to the French colonial era and used as an Ottoman-era forward base south of Tlemcen (16th century).
b_tafraoua-sebdou.etymology_analysis: Hyphenated pairing of Berber Tafraoua ('basin/trough') and Sebdou, two names for the same town in Tlemcen Province.

b_wajda.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 994 AD by Ziri ibn Atiyya, chief of the Zenata Maghrawa tribe.

morphemes.translation: toponym of the Angad plain (traditionally linked to Arabic wajad 'to find' or Berber root)

b_wajda.etymology_analysis: Wajda (modern Oujda) in northeastern Morocco, founded in 994 AD by Ziri ibn Atiyya as a Zenata stronghold near the Algerian border.

older_name_by_867.notes: Traces of a Roman-era Berber settlement exist in the vicinity, but no pre-867 town name is attested.

b_saa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 14th-century Marinid/Zayyanid chronicles (and later Marmol) as Madinat Za ('City of Za') on the Oued Za (predecessor of Taourirt).

morphemes.translation: name of the Oued Za river

b_saa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Oued Za river (a tributary of the Moulouya) in eastern Morocco; the medieval fortified town of Madinat Za preceded modern Taourirt.

b_debdou.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 14th century (Marinid period and 1391 Sephardic Jewish settlement from Seville).
b_debdou.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym Debdou (glossed as 'funnel' in Amazigh), a town in eastern Morocco prominent from the Marinid era onward.

b_bilizma.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in al-Ya'qubi's Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891 AD) as Bilizma, inhabited by tribesmen of Banu Tamim; captured by the Kutama in 905 AD.

morphemes.translation: regional toponym of the Belezma plain and massif

b_bilizma.etymology_analysis: Berber-Arabic toponym Bilizma (Belezma) in the Aurès-Batna region, first documented by al-Ya'qubi in the late 9th century.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Antonine Itinerary and 3rd-century Roman irrigation inscription at Henchir Merouana
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman city of Lamasba (modern Merouana) was the principal ancient urban center of the Belezma plain.

b_baghaya.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 2nd century AD as Roman-Numidian Bagai (with dedications to Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus), continuing as Byzantine Bagaè and Arabic Baghaya.
b_baghaya.etymology_analysis: Arabic Baghaya is the direct phonetic continuation of ancient Numidian-Roman Bagai (Byzantine Bagaè), a major fortified city north of the Aurès Mountains.

older_name_by_867.notes: Baghaya is the direct Arabic continuation of ancient Bagai.

b_biskra.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Arabic geographical sources from the late 9th-10th centuries (al-Ya'qubi / Ibn Hawqal) as Biskra, succeeding Roman Vescera.
b_biskra.etymology_analysis: Biskra evolved phonetically from ancient Roman-Berber Vescera (which remained in use through the 7th-century Battle of Vescera in 683 AD).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder (1st century AD) and Battle of Vescera (683 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman frontier post Vescera (and nearby thermal springs Ad Piscinam) preceded medieval Biskra.

b_badis.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 4th-century Tabula Peutingeriana as Ad Badias and in Roman inscriptions (CIL VIII 17968: ibi ad Bad[ias]).

morphemes.translation: ancient Berber oasis toponym (Latinized as Ad Badias)

b_badis.etymology_analysis: Arabic Badis (Bades) directly continues the ancient Berber-Roman frontier fort name Badias / Ad Badias in the eastern Zab.

older_name_by_867.notes: Badis is the direct continuation of ancient Badias / Ad Badias.

b_sidi_uqba.first_mention_attestation: Mausoleum and mosque of Sidi Uqba (Uqba ibn Nafi, d. 683 AD) established at the site near Thouda in 686 AD.
b_sidi_uqba.eponym_details: Named after Uqba ibn Nafi (d. 683 AD), Umayyad commander of the conquest of the Maghreb, buried there in 683/686 AD.
b_sidi_uqba.etymology_analysis: Arabic honorific toponym Sidi Uqba ('Lord/Saint Uqba'), commemorating the tomb and 686 AD mosque of Umayyad general Uqba ibn Nafi near Biskra.

older_name_by_867.notes: Built near ancient Thouda (Thabudeos), site of the 683 AD battle.

b_waghlanat.first_mention_attestation: Attested c. 1075 AD in Banu Khazrun chronicles when al-Muntasir ibn Khazrun made Waghlana (modern Ourlal) near Biskra his base.
b_waghlanat.etymology_analysis: Berber oasis toponym Waghlana (plural/feminine variant Waghlanat), attested in 11th-century Zirid/Hammadid-era history near Biskra.

b_tubna.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Islamic Tobna (Tubna) by 771 AD during the Kharijite siege of Abbasid governor Umar ibn Hafs, and in al-Ya'qubi (891 AD).
b_tubna.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tubna (Tobna) derives from ancient Numidian-Roman Thubunae / Tubunae, serving as the early Islamic capital of the Zab.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Council of Carthage (256 AD; Bishop Nemesianus of Tubunae)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman-Byzantine city and bishopric Thubunae / Tubunae in Numidia preceded Islamic Tubna.

b_masila.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 924 AD by the Fatimids (al-Qa'im and Ali ibn Hamdun al-Andalusi) in the Hodna plain, originally named al-Muhammadiya.
b_masila.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Masila (modern M'Sila), founded c. 924 AD as a Fatimid stronghold in the western Hodna to replace older Tobna.

older_name_by_867.notes: Roman Zabi (Zabi Justiniana / Bechilga) lay nearby in the Hodna plain.

b_magra.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Arabic by al-Ya'qubi in Kitab al-Buldan (c. 891 AD) as Maqra (Magra), between Barika and M'Sila.
b_magra.etymology_analysis: Arabic Maqra (modern Magra) continues the ancient Roman-Berber settlement name Macri on the Hodna road.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman road itinerary and inscriptions between Thubunae and Zabi
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman settlement Macri occupied the site of modern Magra.

b_ngaous.first_mention_attestation: Attested in medieval Arabic geographical works (11th-12th centuries, e.g., al-Bakri / al-Idrisi) as Niqawus (N'Gaous).

morphemes.translation: Arabicized Berber adaptation of ancient Nicives / Nicivibus

b_ngaous.etymology_analysis: Berber-Arabic N'Gaous (Niqawus) derives from the ancient Numidian-Roman city name Nicives / Nicivibus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: 2nd-3rd century AD Latin votive stelae to Saturn and Council of Carthage (411 AD)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Roman town and bishopric Nicives (Nicivibus) in Numidia stood on the site of modern N'Gaous.
